passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a new cognitive training program on working memory capacity in adults aged 25–35. A randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 participants who were randomly assigned to either the training group (n = 60) or a wait‑list control group (n = 60). Over a 4‑week period, the training group completed 30 minutes of adaptive working‑memory tasks each day, while the control group received no intervention. Working‑memory performance was assessed before and after the intervention using the Digit Span Backward test. The mean pre‑test scores were 7.2 (SD = 1.4) for the training group and 7.1 (SD = 1.5) for the control group. Post‑test scores were 9.6 (SD = 1.3) for the training group and 7.3 (SD = 1.6) for the control group. The researchers reported a statistically significant improvement in the training group compared to controls (p < .001). They concluded that the training program effectively enhances working‑memory capacity in this age group.
stem: Which of the following best describes the main finding of the study?

options.A: The training program had no effect on working‑memory performance.
options.B: The training program improved working‑memory performance compared to controls.
options.C: Both groups improved equally over time.
options.D: The control group outperformed the training group post‑test.

explanation: The post‑test mean for the training group (9.6) was substantially higher than that of the control group (7.3), and the difference was statistically significant (p < .001), indicating the training program’s effectiveness.
trap: Concluding no effect because both groups improved somewhat, ignoring the size of the between-group difference.

stem: Which experimental design element best supports the causal inference that the training program caused the observed improvement?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to groups
options.B: Use of a Digit Span Backward test

explanation: Random assignment controls for confounding variables, allowing the researchers to attribute differences between groups to the intervention.
trap: Crediting the p-value or the test instrument rather than random assignment for causal inference.

stem: What is the approximate effect size (Cohen's d) for the difference between the post-test means of the training and control groups?
explanation: Cohen's d = (9.6 - 7.3)/SDpooled; SDpooled = sqrt[(1.3² + 1.6²)/2] = 1.46. d = 2.3/1.46 = 1.58, a very large effect.
trap: Dividing by the wrong SD or using a pre-test/post-test difference within the training group alone.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the data in the passage?

options.A: Mean pre-test scores were similar in the training and control groups.
options.B: The training group’s mean score rose by 2.4 points from pre-test to post-test.
options.C: The control group’s mean score rose by 0.2 points from pre-test to post-test.
options.D: The post-test SD was smaller in the control group than in the training group.

explanation: Correct: The post-test SDs were 1.3 (training) and 1.6 (control), so the control SD was larger. Why the others are wrong: A) pre-test means were 7.2 and 7.1. B) 9.6 - 7.2 = 2.4. C) 7.3 - 7.1 = 0.2.
trap: Assuming the group that changed little must also have the smaller spread.

stem: Which of the following best links this study to broader cognitive‑enhancement research?

options.A: It demonstrates that physical exercise is superior to cognitive training.
options.B: It supports the theory that working‑memory capacity is malleable with targeted practice.
options.C: It refutes the concept of transfer effects between different cognitive domains.
options.D: It indicates that age is the sole determinant of working‑memory decline.

explanation: The study provides evidence that working‑memory can be improved through specific training, aligning with the malleability hypothesis in cognitive‑enhancement literature.
trap: Reading the result as refuting transfer or as showing physical exercise is better, which the study did not test.
